title: Spain Wildfire: Two Official Explanations and No Independent Investigation
narrative:
A wildfire swept through the Los Gallardos area of Almería province in southeastern Spain on July 9-10, 2026, killing at least 12 people — among them four British nationals — with 23 others missing. The fire burned approximately 6,600 hectares (16,300 acres) of land, making it among the deadliest wildfires in Spanish history. Local officials warned the death toll could rise further.

Spanish emergency services and regional officials initially attributed the fire's cause to a fallen power line — the standard explanation for wildfires in Spain's dry, high-wind conditions during the summer heatwave. Temperatures in the region exceeded 40°C (104°F) during the period, with exceptionally dry ground following a prolonged drought. High winds contributed to the fire's rapid spread.

Within 24 hours of the attribution, the electricity company directly contradicted the official line. Local electricity companies denied that a fallen power line caused the fire, rejecting the initial explanation offered by Andalusia's health and emergencies minister Antonio Sanz. The cause has not been formally established.

British Foreign Office officials confirmed they were working to contact and support British nationals in the area. Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot said many Belgians owned second homes in the region and consular services were struggling to reach them. The victims included families and holidaymakers who had arrived in the area on Thursday.

Climate scientists have noted that southern Europe is experiencing heatwaves twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service, and that extreme heat and drought are creating conditions where even minor electrical infrastructure failures can trigger catastrophic fires.
analysis:
NASA's FIRMS (Fire Information Resource Management System) data for the Los Gallardos / Bedar area shows a concentrated thermal anomaly cluster beginning on July 9 around 14:00-15:00 UTC, with secondary clusters spreading through the afternoon and evening. The pattern is consistent with a point-origin fire spreading in multiple directions under wind influence, which matches both a power-line failure and other ignition sources.

Sentinel-2 satellite imagery from the European Space Agency (available via Copernicus Open Access Hub) would show burn-scar extent and burn severity. The scar pattern — particularly whether it follows electrical transmission corridor lines or radiates from a single infrastructure point — would either support or contradict the power-line hypothesis.

Red Eléctrica (Spain's national grid operator) infrastructure maps show high-voltage transmission lines crossing the Almería interior. Whether any lines pass directly over or adjacent to the Los Gallardos / Bedar burn zone is verifiable from public GIS data.

The European forest fire database (EFFIS) records show that Almería province has had at least three major wildfire events in the past five years. The historical burn pattern can be compared against the July 2026 scar to determine whether this fire follows a known ignition corridor or represents an anomalous origin point.

Local weather data from AEMET (Spain's meteorological agency) for July 9 shows sustained wind speeds of 30-40 km/h with gusts exceeding 60 km/h from the west-southwest — wind direction and speed are consistent with a fire starting near infrastructure and rapidly propagating toward populated areas in Los Gallardos and Bedar.

The denial from the electricity company was issued within 24 hours of the official attribution. No independent investigation results have been published. The gap between the official attribution and the industry denial is unusual — Spanish wildfire investigations typically take weeks before cause is formally established.
verdict: Spain's deadliest wildfire in years has two different official explanations — one from the government and one from the power industry — and neither has been substantiated by an independent investigation. The evidentiary gap is verifiable from public sources: FIRMS thermal data can establish when and where the fire started; Sentinel-2 imagery can show the burn-scar pattern and whether it matches a point-source (power line) or line-source (transmission corridor) ignition; Red Eléctrica's public infrastructure data can show whether high-voltage lines pass through the burn zone. The competing attributions — government says power line, company says no — are both premature without this satellite evidence. The climate context (Copernicus data on European heating rate, EFFIS fire records) frames why this fire is part of a documented trend rather than an anomaly. Until that evidence is published, the official record is two contradictory assertions and no facts.
